name: Length Contraction
what: This subtopic covers proper length, contracted length, and the application of L = L₀/γ. It examines which observer measures the proper length and how contraction only occurs in the direction of relative motion.
why: Length contraction is the spatial counterpart of time dilation. Together they ensure that all observers measure the same speed of light. Length contraction also has direct engineering consequences — particle accelerator drift tubes must be designed with it in mind.

items.title: I can define proper length (L₀) and identify which observer measures it
items.what: Proper length is the length of an object or distance measured by an observer who is at rest relative to the object or the two points defining the length. It is always the longest length measurement for that object.
items.why: Identifying who measures proper length is the critical first step for length contraction problems. Getting this wrong leads to an answer that is longer than the proper length, which is physically impossible.
items.example: A rocket crew measures the length of their own rocket to be 100 m. Since they are at rest relative to the rocket, this is the proper length. An Earth observer watching the rocket fly past measures a shorter, contracted length.

items.title: I can define contracted length (L) and explain why it is shorter than proper length
items.what: Contracted length is the length of a moving object or distance measured by an observer in relative motion with respect to that object. It is always less than the proper length for the same object.
items.why: Length contraction follows directly from the constancy of the speed of light and the definition of simultaneity. It is not an optical illusion — it is a real physical consequence of relative motion.
items.example: A platform is 500 m long as measured by a person standing on it (proper length). A rocket crew passing at 0.866c (γ = 2) measures the platform to be 500 / 2 = 250 m long.

items.title: I can apply the length contraction formula L = L₀/γ to various situations
items.what: The equation L = L₀/γ relates proper length L₀ to contracted length L. Since γ ≥ 1, contracted length is always ≤ proper length. Rearranging gives L₀ = Lγ, which is used when the contracted length is given and the proper length is unknown.
items.why: This formula is used directly in VCE exam questions involving rockets, platforms, particle accelerators, and muon travel distances.
items.example: A rocket of proper length 200 m passes Earth at 0.700c (γ = 1.40). The Earth observer measures its length as L = 200 / 1.40 = 143 m.

items.title: I can state that length contraction only occurs in the direction of relative motion
items.what: Special relativity predicts that an object contracts only along the axis parallel to its direction of travel relative to the observer. Dimensions perpendicular to the direction of motion are unchanged.
items.why: This is a common point of confusion. Students sometimes incorrectly apply length contraction to all dimensions of an object.
items.example: A square spacecraft 50 m × 50 m moving horizontally at 0.866c (γ = 2) is measured by an Earth observer to be 25 m long in the direction of travel but still 50 m wide.

items.title: I can calculate the speed of an object given its proper length and contracted length
items.what: By finding γ = L₀ / L from measured lengths, and then rearranging γ to solve for v, the relative speed between two frames can be determined from length measurements.
items.why: This tests the same algebraic reasoning as the reverse time dilation calculation and is a common exam question style.
items.example: A rocket's proper length is 60.0 m. An observer measures it as 14.0 m. γ = 60.0 / 14.0 = 4.286. Then v = c × √(1 − 1/4.286²) = 0.971c.

items.title: I can explain what happens to contracted length as relative speed increases
items.what: As relative speed increases, γ increases, so the contracted length decreases further. As v approaches c, the contracted length approaches zero.
items.why: This qualitative understanding is needed for graph-based questions and for checking whether calculated answers are physically reasonable.
items.example: At v = 0.5c (γ ≈ 1.15), a 100 m rocket appears 87 m long. At v = 0.99c (γ ≈ 7.09), the same rocket appears only 14 m long to an external observer.

items.title: I can explain why particle accelerator drift tubes must account for length contraction
items.what: In a linear accelerator (linac), charged particles travel through a series of drift tubes. The timing of the alternating voltage is set to match the time the particle spends inside each tube. Since particles travel at relativistic speeds, the drift tubes are contracted in the particle's reference frame — engineers must design tube lengths based on this contracted measurement.
items.why: If length contraction were ignored in the design, the alternating voltage would switch at the wrong moment, decelerating the particle rather than accelerating it. This is a direct, practical application of special relativity.
items.example: A proton at 0.995c (γ = 10) passes through a drift tube that is 85.5 cm long in the particle's frame. The proper length of the tube as measured in the lab is 85.5 × 10 = 855 mm = 85.5 cm × 10 = 85.5 cm × γ = 85.5 cm in the particle frame, so L₀ = 85.5 × 10 = 855 mm.
